progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m8-c03a and chem-m8-c03b (see Scope); chem-m5-p03 (the well plate, black card, dropper tip above the well); skills-s07 (aim, variables, validity, reliability, accuracy; word, feature, fix); chem-m5-c13 (net ionic equations).
progression.startsWith: Here's a result that nearly fooled a student. She's testing unknown C for chloride. She acidifies a few drops with nitric acid, adds silver nitrate, and a faint white cloud appears. Chloride? But in the next well, she'd put plain water and the same reagents, and that well went cloudy too. If the water does it, the cloud can't prove anything about the unknown. She'd rinsed the plate with tap water, and tap water carries a little chloride. That one extra well saved her conclusion.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the aim and variables of a qualitative ion investigation; setting up a blank and a known for each reagent; rinsing with distilled water; running small-scale tests on a well plate with the right backgrounds; running a blank flame; recording observations before inferences; justifying each identity with an observation, an equation, what was ruled out and a matching known; stating that no visible change means not detected; judging validity, reliability and accuracy for an identity; writing the risk rows for silver nitrate, barium salts (and why lead results come as data), acids and alkali, ammonia, the hot loop, and the waste.
progression.nextLesson: once you know which ion is there, how much is there? (route chem-m8-c04, colour and absorption).

teaching.task: Every well with silver nitrate went cloudy, even the one with no unknown in it. How do you plan, run and record qualitative tests so that each identity you report would stand up, and do it safely?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a cloud in the blank means the reagent, water or equipment, not the unknown, caused it; tap water carries chloride (1); (2) the aim, the plan from the two flowcharts, and the variables (2); (3) blank and known, and why each is needed; one row per reagent; distilled water (3); (4) small scale: less hazardous material and waste; dropper tip above the well; backgrounds; labelled grid (4); (5) unknown C's cation tests, the blank flame, the known magnesium match (5); (6) unknown C's anion tests; the clear blank shows no chloride (6); (7) recording: observation before inference, "no visible change", changes with time (7); (8) justification: observation, equation, what was ruled out, the known; no visible change means not detected (8); (9) valid, reliable, accurate for an identity (9); (10) hazards and controls, waste (10); memory aid (11); attempts (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Here's a result that nearly fooled a student. The aim: identify the cation and the anion in each of four unknown solutions, where each holds one of each from the syllabus lists. Now the controls. Run it small. Unknown C, cation first, fresh drops in each well. Then the anion, again with fresh drops. Record as you go, in a table you drew up before you started. When you report an identity, give the evidence and the chemistry. Now the three words from the practical skills video. Now the risks. One line for every reagent: blank, known, unknown. Your turn. Not valid. Last one. Calcium chloride. So, for any unknown: plan the tests from the flowcharts, run blank, known and unknown side by side at small scale, record what you see before what it means, and justify each identity with an observation and an equation.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's a result that nearly fooled a student. She's testing unknown C for chloride. She acidifies a few drops with nitric acid, adds silver nitrate, and a faint white cloud appears. Chloride? But in the next well, she'd put plain water and the same reagents, and that well went cloudy too. If the water does it, the cloud can't prove anything about the unknown. She'd rinsed the plate with tap water, and tap water carries a little chloride. That one extra well saved her conclusion.
teaching.understandingCheck: Two, each 10 s with the countdown and every condition visible (12, 14): A1's single loop, the water rinse, four blue-green flames and the conclusion; A2's seven results with the blank and known entries. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.
teaching.curriculumScope:
Syllabus dotpoint (as printed; NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p57; C8-IQ1-02 is this project's local catalogue ID, not a code printed in the syllabus), quoted from ../../programme/syllabus/chem-2017-y12.json:

"conduct qualitative investigations – using flame tests, precipitation and complexation reactions as appropriate – to test for the presence in aqueous solution of the following ions:
- cations: barium (Ba2+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+), lead(II) (Pb2+), silver ion (Ag+), copper(II) (Cu2+), iron(II) (Fe2+), iron(III) (Fe3+)
- anions: chloride (Cl–), bromide (Br–), iodide (I–), hydroxide (OH–), acetate (CH3COO–), carbonate (CO32–), sulfate (SO42–), phosphate (PO43–)"

(The two dashes in the first line are en dashes as printed, not em dashes.) The tests themselves were chem-m8-c03a (cations) and chem-m8-c03b (anions). This video is the investigation: planning it, running it safely at small scale, recording it and justifying the identities.

design.visualSystem: no people, hands or faces (drops, the wire loop, wafting and rinsing are coded motion); apparatus as painted plates listed by filename, never stretched; any test tube that appears is from the aligned m5x rack set (alpha bounds 568, 200, 1432, 1800); well contents are coded fills over the painted well plate (the chem-m5-p03 method, already published); at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one reasoning stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card in the attempts, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; real GHS classifications, schools' own risk assessments named in the footer; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("usually", "points to", "supports"); optional key notes hold.
